stories.summary: A Seoul court sentenced Han Hak-ja, leader of the Unification Church, to two years for bribing the wife of ousted president Yoon Suk Yeol — the transfers included two Chanel bags and a diamond necklace alongside political funding offences. Lead with the smallness of the objects against the size of the access purchased: a religious movement buying a channel into the presidential residence. The accountability angle is that the court reached the church rather than only the politician, and it lands while Yoon's own removal is still being litigated. Note what the sentence does and does not settle about the first lady's own liability.

stories.label: Kazakhstan's president appoints top adviser as vice president
stories.summary: Tokayev filled the vice presidency — an office that did not exist until the new constitution took effect — with Erlan Karin, previously state counsellor and first deputy head of the presidential administration. The mechanism worth explaining: a constitutional amendment created a succession slot, and the first occupant is the president's own long-serving ideologist, not an elected figure. For a reader watching Central Asia, this is how managed succession is engineered in advance of a transition rather than during one — the same problem Nazarbayev's exit posed, addressed structurally this time. Note that the feed carried no Kazakh outlet on this.

stories.label: Egypt pushes for a settlement in Libya
stories.summary: Cairo is trying to bridge Libya's eastern and western governments and, more consequentially, to unify the two rival military institutions. Who holds power: Egypt, which borders Libya and has backed the eastern LNA, now positioning itself as the broker rather than a party. The mechanism readers should grasp is sequencing — military unification before or after a political settlement is the question every previous Libya process has failed on, and it is the same sequencing problem the UN envoy faces in Sudan. Written from Cairo, which is the perspective the story is usually told without.

stories.label: From Bombay Time To IST: How India Finally Agreed On One Clock
stories.summary: India notified the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026, making IST the single legally binding reference for banks, exchanges, telecom operators and the power grid. This is infrastructure law, not a curiosity: trade settlement, grid synchronisation and telecom billing all depend on an agreed timestamp, and until now India's legal position on which clock governs was ambiguous. Lead with what breaks when two systems disagree by milliseconds. The Bombay Time history is the hook, not the story — the story is that a billion-person economy just made time a regulated quantity.

stories.label: How Pakistan's budget is making nutritious food unaffordable
stories.summary: Dawn traces the transmission from fiscal policy to the plate: when purchasing power falls, households do not eat less — they eat worse, cutting protein and micronutrient-dense food first while keeping calories up on cheap staples. Who is affected: Pakistani households already at the margin. The mechanism to lead with is that a calorie-adequate diet can still be a nutritionally failing one, which is why headline food-security numbers miss this entirely. Connects to the Punjab clinic-sealing story from the previous cycle — both are the health cost of a squeezed budget arriving through different doors.

stories.label: Bangladesh wants Nepal's power, but India holds the key
stories.summary: Bangladesh wants to buy Nepali hydropower and Nepal wants to sell it, but the electricity must cross Indian transmission lines — and three governments have been stalled over a mere 20 MW, a rounding error on any national grid. Lead with that number against the size of the stalemate. The structural point is transit power: whoever owns the wires between two countries holds a veto over their trade, and South Asia's renewable build-out depends on interconnection India controls. Who bears the cost: Bangladeshi consumers buying more expensive thermal power instead.

stories.label: Death toll from deadly Nepal floods rises to over 5,000
stories.summary: Nepal's Home Ministry now puts the flood death toll above 5,000 — by a wide margin the largest loss of life in this cycle's feed, and it is carried by almost no one. Lead with the count and with the fact of the silence around it. The mechanism: Himalayan catchments concentrate monsoon runoff into narrow valleys where the settlement is, so a rainfall anomaly becomes a mass-casualty event within hours rather than days. Attribute the figure precisely to the Home Ministry and flag that tolls at this stage are still rising and provisional.

stories.label: Should we all be taking low doses of lithium to prevent Alzheimer's?
stories.summary: The question is whether trace lithium — the kind already present in some groundwater at doses far below psychiatric prescribing — is protective against dementia. Lead with the dose gap, which is the whole story: the psychiatric dose and the hypothesised protective dose differ by orders of magnitude, and evidence at the low end is largely epidemiological, not trial-based. The reader should leave knowing exactly what is established and what is not, and why 'it is in the water already' is an argument about correlation. Do not let the 1880s Texas well anecdote lead; it is the least reliable thing in the piece.

stories.label: Omarchy: Any User Process Can Escalate to Root
stories.summary: A widely promoted Linux desktop distribution shipped a configuration in which any unprivileged user process can obtain root. Lead with the mechanism — how the credential is reachable — not with the vendor's name, because the general lesson is the one that transfers: opinionated 'batteries-included' distributions inherit the security posture of whoever assembled the defaults, and users who chose it for convenience have no way to audit that. 488 points and 473 comments on Hacker News is the signal that practitioners recognise it as a class of failure, not a one-off.

stories.label: Zcash private transactions could go from three-second waits to under 200 milliseconds
stories.summary: New cryptography tooling cuts the wallet-side cost of building a shielded Zcash transaction from about three seconds to under 200 milliseconds — and requires no network upgrade, which is the detail to lead with. The structural point: privacy on a blockchain has always been priced in latency and compute, and that price is what pushed users onto transparent addresses. A 15x reduction changes the default. Frame the 50,000-transactions-per-second target as the stated ambition it is, not as an achieved figure.

stories.label: Toward next-generation computing through ferroelectricity
stories.summary: A review of what actually gates ferroelectric computing — the candidate successor to charge-based memory and logic — and the answer is that no single material parameter decides it. Remanent polarisation, Curie temperature, coercive field, switching speed and endurance trade against each other, so the choice is application-specific rather than a race one material wins. Lead with that: readers are used to semiconductor stories with a winner, and this is a story about why there isn't one. Keep it concrete about what ferroelectric memory would buy — non-volatility without the write-energy penalty.
